stage2_post.text:
Keeping experiment records helps engineers because it creates a reliable memory of what was actually tried, observed, and measured. Engineering work often involves many variables, repeated trials, and small adjustments, so without written records it becomes easy to misremember which configuration produced a given result. Detailed records allow engineers to reproduce an experiment later, which is essential for verifying that a result is real rather than a one-time anomaly. They also help engineers compare alternatives systematically, since recorded data can be reviewed side by side instead of relying on impression or recollection. When something fails, records make it possible to trace the sequence of decisions and conditions that led to the failure, which speeds up diagnosis and prevents the same mistake from being repeated. Records also support collaboration, because colleagues can understand what has already been done and build on it without duplicating effort. In addition, they provide evidence for design decisions, safety reviews, patents, and regulatory or quality requirements. Over time, well-kept records become a valuable knowledge base that helps engineers improve processes, justify conclusions, and transfer experience to future projects.

stage2_post_pre.text:
Keeping experiment records helps engineers because it creates a reliable memory of what was actually tried, observed, and measured. Engineering work often involves many variables, repeated trials, and long gaps between sessions, so without written records it is easy to forget important details or misremember results. Clear records allow engineers to reproduce an experiment later, which is essential for verifying that a result is real and not a one-time anomaly. They also help engineers compare different approaches fairly, since the recorded conditions and measurements provide a consistent basis for evaluation. When something fails, records make it easier to trace the cause by showing exactly what changed and when. Records also support collaboration, because other team members can understand prior work without having to repeat it or rely on someone's memory. In addition, good documentation protects against lost time and wasted effort by preventing engineers from redoing experiments they have already completed. Over time, accumulated records become a valuable knowledge base that can inform future designs and decisions. Finally, keeping records supports accountability and professionalism, since it shows that conclusions are based on evidence rather than guesswork.
